rejected.title: Causes of wellbeing differences
card: Wellbeing is how well people live: their health, education, income and safety. It differs between countries and within them, and several causes work together to shape it.
Resources matter. A place with fertile land, clean water or minerals has more to build on, if it can use them well.
Services and work matter. Health and education services help people live longer and learn skills. Jobs and income let families pay for food, housing and care.

Technology and government matter too. Technology such as the internet and modern machines can lift output and access to services. Governments decide how money is raised and spent, and their choices can widen or narrow gaps.
rejected.remember: Wellbeing gaps come from several causes working together, not from one cause alone.

a.q: A mine in a small town closes and hundreds of workers lose their jobs. Which effect on wellbeing is most likely?
opts: Families have less income for food, housing and care
Wellbeing rises, as workers now have more free time
Wellbeing holds steady, as the minerals are still there
Wellbeing falls mainly because the town loses its schools
a.why: Jobs bring income, and income pays for food, housing and care, so losing jobs is likely to lower wellbeing. The minerals staying in the ground does not help, because resources only add to wellbeing when they are put to use.
a.clue: Trace what losing work means for a household.

b.q: Country X has large mineral deposits, but most people have low incomes and few clinics. Which explanation fits the card best?
opts: Its minerals may not be used well to fund services and jobs
It needs to find more minerals before wellbeing can rise
Its wellbeing is low because it lacks natural resources
Its wellbeing is measured by minerals, not health or income
b.why: Resources give a place more to build on, but people benefit only if the resources are used well, for example through government spending on clinics and jobs. Finding more minerals is tempting, but Country X already has plenty, so having more would not fix how they are used.
b.clue: Having resources and using them well are different things.

draft.title: Causes of wellbeing differences
card: Wellbeing is how well people live: their health, education, income and safety. It differs between countries and also within them.
Resources matter. A place with fertile land, clean water or minerals has more to build on, though it must be able to use them well.
Services and work matter. Health and education services help people live longer and learn skills. Jobs and income let families buy food, housing and care.

Technology and government matter too. Technology such as the internet and modern machines can lift output and access to services. Governments decide how money is raised and spent, and their choices can widen or narrow gaps.
draft.remember: Wellbeing gaps come from several causes working together, not from one cause alone.

a.q: Which change is most likely to improve wellbeing in a region where many children leave school early?
opts: Building more schools and training more teachers
Raising the price of imported goods
Moving the region's capital city to the coast
Building a larger sports stadium in the region
a.why: Education services help people gain skills, which can lead to better jobs and income. The other changes do not directly improve access to education.
a.clue: Which change gives children more chance to learn?

b.q: Country X has large mineral deposits but most people have low incomes and few clinics. Which explanation fits best with the card?
opts: Minerals help only if used to fund services and jobs
Minerals alone set wellbeing, so Country X is doing well
Mineral wealth cuts wellbeing because it removes jobs
Technology sets wellbeing, so resources cannot matter
b.why: Resources give a place more to build on, but government choices, services and jobs decide whether people benefit. The tempting option says resources alone set wellbeing, but the card shows several causes work together.
b.clue: Having resources and using them well are different things.

a.best: Building more schools and training more teachers

b.best: Minerals help only if used to fund services and jobs

problems.detail: The right option says minerals help 'only if used to fund services and jobs'. The card says resources give a place more to build on if they are used well, and they could also help through technology or government income. 'Only' and the narrow list go beyond the card. Better: 'Minerals help when they are used well to fund services and jobs'.

The right option is the only balanced, conditional statement. The other three are extreme absolutes ('cuts wellbeing', 'alone set', 'cannot matter'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

Too easy for Year 10. The distractors (a sports stadium, import prices, moving the capital) have no plausible link to early school leaving, and the clue ('more chance to learn') points straight at the answer.

Services and work matter. Health and education services help people live longer and learn skills. Jobs and income let families pay for food, housing and care.

Technology and government matter too. Technology such as the internet and modern machines can lift output and access to services. Governments decide how money is raised and spent, and their choices can widen or narrow gaps.
version.remember: Wellbeing gaps come from several causes working together, not from one cause alone.

a.q: Hundreds of workers lose their jobs when a small town's mine closes. What is the most likely effect on wellbeing in the town?
opts: Wellbeing falls, as households lose their income
Wellbeing rises, as workers now have more free time
Wellbeing holds steady, as the minerals are still there
Wellbeing rises, as the land is no longer being mined
a.why: Jobs bring income, and income pays for food, housing and care, so losing jobs is likely to lower wellbeing. The minerals still being in the ground does not keep wellbeing steady, because a place gains from resources when it can use them well.
a.clue: Trace what losing work means for a household.

b.q: Country Z has rich mineral deposits, yet most of its people earn little and have few clinics nearby. Which explanation fits best?
opts: Its mineral wealth may not be reaching services and jobs
It may need to find more minerals before wellbeing rises
Its wellbeing may be low because it lacks natural resources
Its wellbeing may be judged by minerals, not by health
b.why: Resources give a place more to build on if it can use them well, for example by spending mineral income on clinics and jobs. Here the wealth may not be reaching people. Finding more minerals is tempting, but Country Z already has plenty, so more would not change how they are used.
b.clue: Country Z has the resources. What might stop people gaining from them?

a.best: Wellbeing falls, as households lose their income

b.best: Its mineral wealth may not be reaching services and jobs
